Time-varying-parameter VARs with stochastic volatility

Source: vignettes/tvp-var.Rmd
tvp-var.Rmd

tvpvar() estimates a VAR whose coefficients, contemporaneous (impact) matrix and shock volatilities all drift over time (Cogley and Sargent, 2005; Primiceri, 2005), using the Gibbs-sampler ordering of Del Negro and Primiceri (2015). It answers the questions that a constant-parameter VAR cannot: did the transmission mechanism change (for example the response to a monetary policy shock), and did the size of shocks change (the Great Moderation)?

It is also the model in this package where the prior matters most. Section 6 documents, with simulations, how the results depend on the prior tightness and when time variation can be found where none exists. Read it before interpreting any estimated drift.

A first look (the sections below explain each object):

fit <- tvpvar(yt, p = 2, ndraw = 2000, nburn = 1000)
autoplot(fit, "vol")                          # volatility paths
irf(fit, date = c(1975, 2000), horizon = 16)  # impulse responses at two dates

1. The model

Let xt=(yt−1′,…,yt−p′,1)′x_t=(y_{t-1}',\dots,y_{t-p}',1)' (m=Kp+1m=Kp+1 regressors) and let BtB_t be the m×Km\times K matrix of coefficients with βt=vec(Bt)\beta_t=\mathrm{vec}(B_t) (equation by equation). The model, in the notation of the code, is yt=(IK⊗xt′)βt+ut,ut=At−1Λt1/2εt,εt∼N(0,IK),βt=βt−1+ηt,ηt∼N(0,Q),αt=αt−1+ζt,ζt∼N(0,S),S=blockdiag(S2,…,SK),hit=hi,t−1+νit,νit∼N(0,Wi),hit=ln⁡λit.\begin{align} y_t&=(I_K\otimes x_t')\,\beta_t+u_t, & u_t&=A_t^{-1}\Lambda_t^{1/2}\varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,I_K),\\ \beta_t&=\beta_{t-1}+\eta_t, & \eta_t&\sim N(0,Q),\\ \alpha_t&=\alpha_{t-1}+\zeta_t, & \zeta_t&\sim N(0,S),\ S=\mathrm{blockdiag}(S_2,\dots,S_K),\\ h_{it}&=h_{i,t-1}+\nu_{it}, & \nu_{it}&\sim N(0,W_i),\quad h_{it}=\ln\lambda_{it}. \end{align}AtA_t is unit lower triangular with free elements αt\alpha_t (the K(K−1)/2K(K-1)/2 elements below the diagonal, equation by equation), Λt=diag(eh1t,…,ehKt)\Lambda_t=\mathrm{diag}(e^{h_{1t}},\dots,e^{h_{Kt}}) and Σt=At−1ΛtAt−1′\Sigma_t=A_t^{-1}\Lambda_tA_t^{-1\prime} is the time-varying reduced-form covariance. So uit=−∑j<iαij,tujt+ehit/2εitu_{it}=-\sum_{j<i}\alpha_{ij,t}u_{jt}+e^{h_{it}/2}\varepsilon_{it}, a recursive (Cholesky) structure with time-varying impact coefficients and shock sizes.

Three distinct kinds of time variation, with different economics:

state what moves interpretation
βt\beta_t (covariance QQ) lag coefficients the transmission mechanism: for example a policy rule that reacts more to inflation after Volcker
hth_t (innovation variances WiW_i) size of the structural shocks the Great Moderation, 2008, 2020
αt\alpha_t (covariance SS) contemporaneous coefficients how shocks spread within the quarter

Differences from Primiceri (2005) worth knowing: hith_{it} is the log variance (so eh/2e^{h/2} is the standard deviation), all states are pure random walks (no mean reversion and, by default, no stationarity restriction) and the states at the first estimation date have the prior given below. Special cases are obtained with flags: tv_A = FALSE is Cogley and Sargent (2005); sv = FALSE, tv_A = FALSE is Cogley and Sargent (2001) with homoskedastic errors; tv_beta = FALSE freezes the coefficients, which gives a Bayesian VAR with SV, the benchmark against which to judge whether time-varying coefficients are needed at all (section 6).

2. The training-sample prior and its hyperparameters

The prior of Primiceri (2005) is calibrated on a training sample, the first tau effective observations (after the first pp lags; they are not part of the estimation sample, so with T=215T=215, p=2p=2 and τ=40\tau=40 the estimation sample is 173 quarters, 1963Q3-2006Q2). On the training sample compute B̂=(X′X)−1X′Y\hat B=(X'X)^{-1}X'Y, Σ̂=Û′Û/(τ−m)\hat\Sigma=\hat U'\hat U/(\tau-m) and V(B̂)=Σ̂⊗(X′X)−1V(\hat B)=\hat\Sigma\otimes(X'X)^{-1}; regress each OLS residual ûi\hat u_i on û1,…,ûi−1\hat u_{1},\dots,\hat u_{i-1} to get α̂i=−(coefficients)\hat\alpha_i=-(\text{coefficients}) with covariance V(α̂i)=v̂i(Ei′Ei)−1V(\hat\alpha_i)=\hat v_i(E_i'E_i)^{-1}, and let σ̂i2\hat\sigma_i^2 be the residual variance of the ii-th such regression (v̂i\hat v_i). Then (tvp_train()): β1∼N(B̂,cV(B̂)),α1∼N(α̂,cV(α̂)),hi0∼N(ln⁡σ̂i2,10),Q∼IW(kQ2νQV(B̂),νQ),Si∼IW(kS2(1+dim⁡Si)V(α̂i),1+dim⁡Si),Wi∼IG(1,kW2),\begin{align} \beta_1&\sim N\big(\hat B,\ c\,V(\hat B)\big), & \alpha_1&\sim N\big(\hat\alpha,\ c\,V(\hat\alpha)\big), & h_{i0}&\sim N(\ln\hat\sigma_i^2,\ 10),\\ Q&\sim IW\big(k_Q^2\,\nu_Q\,V(\hat B),\ \nu_Q\big), & S_i&\sim IW\big(k_S^2\,(1+\dim S_i)\,V(\hat\alpha_i),\ 1+\dim S_i\big), & W_i&\sim IG(1,\ k_W^2), \end{align} with c=c=vscale (4), νQ=\nu_Q=df_Q (default τ\tau), dim⁡Si=i−1\dim S_i=i-1, and IG(a,b)IG(a,b) with shape aa and scale bb. The hyperparameters, in tvp_prior(tau = 40, kQ = 0.01, kS = 0.1, kW = 0.01, ...):

  • tau: training-sample length. It sets the scale of V(B̂)V(\hat B) (a short sample means large standard errors, hence a looser prior on the level of β1\beta_1 and, through V(B̂)V(\hat B), a larger prior on drift) and the default degrees of freedom.
  • kQ: scales the prior of the coefficient drift. E[Q]=kQ2νQ/(νQ−nβ−1)V(B̂)E[Q]=k_Q^2\nu_Q/(\nu_Q-n_\beta-1)\ V(\hat B) with nβ=mKn_\beta=mK states, so the prior standard deviation of the quarterly change of coefficient jj is about kQνQ/(νQ−nβ−1)k_Q\sqrt{\nu_Q/(\nu_Q-n_\beta-1)} times its training-sample standard error. For K=3K=3, p=2p=2 (nβ=21n_\beta=21, νQ=40\nu_Q=40) that factor is 1.5kQ1.5k_Q. Note that E[Q]E[Q] exists only if νQ>nβ+1\nu_Q>n_\beta+1 (and the prior is proper only if νQ≥nβ\nu_Q\ge n_\beta): for p=4p=4, nβ=39n_\beta=39 and the default df_Q = 40 leaves the prior mean of QQ undefined. tvpvar() only checks that tau exceeds m+Km+K (and that enough observations remain after the training sample), not this condition on νQ\nu_Q, so it is up to you to raise tau or df_Q.
  • kS, kW: same role for the drift of the impact coefficients and the log-variances (WiW_i is a variance, so kW=0.01k_W=0.01 means a prior scale of 10−410^{-4}, i.e. quarterly standard deviation of hh of order 0.01 to 0.1 once the likelihood is added).
  • vscale, h_var: prior inflation of the initial state; they matter little.
fit0 <- tvpvar(yt, p = 2, ndraw = 300, nburn = 200, nsave_paths = 50)   # throw-away fit to inspect the prior
pv <- fit0$prior_values
nb <- fit0$m * fit0$K
round(sqrt(diag(pv$Qbar)[1:7] / (pv$nuQ - nb - 1)), 4)   # prior sd of the quarterly drift, equation 1 (7 coefficients)
#> [1] 0.0019 0.0011 0.0013 0.0018 0.0011 0.0012 0.0035

3. The Gibbs sampler

One sweep draws, in this order (src/tvp.cpp):

  1. Coefficients βT∣AT,ΛT,Q,Y\beta^T\mid A^T,\Lambda^T,Q,Y. Conditionally this is a linear Gaussian state-space model, yt=Ztβt+uty_t=Z_t\beta_t+u_t, Zt=IK⊗xt′Z_t=I_K\otimes x_t', ut∼N(0,Σt)u_t\sim N(0,\Sigma_t), βt=βt−1+ηt\beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+\eta_t. The path is drawn with the Durbin and Koopman (2002) simulation smoother:
    1. simulate (β+,y+)(\beta^+,y^+) from the model with the prior mean replaced by zero;
    2. compute yt*=yt−Ztb0−yt+y^*_t=y_t-Z_tb_0-y^+_t and run the Kalman filter and the backward smoothing recursion on y*y^* to get β̂t*=E[βt∣y*]\hat\beta^*_t=E[\beta_t\mid y^*];
    3. set β̃t=b0+βt++β̂t*\tilde\beta_t=b_0+\beta^+_t+\hat\beta^*_t, which is an exact draw from p(βT∣⋅)p(\beta^T\mid\cdot) by linearity of the smoother. The advantage over the Carter and Kohn (1994) backward sampler used by Primiceri is that the filter only inverts the K×KK\times K innovation variance (cost O(Tns2K)O(T\,n_s^2K) for ns=mKn_s=mK states) rather than factorising an ns×nsn_s\times n_s conditional state covariance at every date (O(Tns3)O(Tn_s^3)), and that no Cholesky of a near-singular state covariance is needed when QQ is tiny.
  2. Impact coefficients αT∣βT,ΛT,S\alpha^T\mid\beta^T,\Lambda^T,S, equation by equation. With ut=yt−Ztβtu_t=y_t-Z_t\beta_t the ii-th equation is uit=−u<i,t′αi,t+ehit/2εitu_{it}=-u_{<i,t}'\alpha_{i,t}+e^{h_{it}/2}\varepsilon_{it}, again linear Gaussian in the random-walk state αi,t\alpha_{i,t} (observation matrix −u<i,t′-u_{<i,t}', variance ehite^{h_{it}}), drawn with the same smoother. Block-diagonality of SS is what makes the rows independent.
  3. Volatilities (sT,hT)∣βT,αT(s^T,h^T)\mid\beta^T,\alpha^T. The orthogonalised residual eit=uit+∑j<iαij,tujt=ehit/2εite_{it}=u_{it}+\sum_{j<i}\alpha_{ij,t}u_{jt}=e^{h_{it}/2}\varepsilon_{it} gives ln⁡(eit2+10−4)=hit+ln⁡εit2\ln(e_{it}^2+10^{-4})=h_{it}+\ln\varepsilon_{it}^2; the log-chi-squared error is approximated by the 10-component mixture of Omori et al. (2007), with mixture indicators drawn first (given the current hh) and then the path by forward-filtering backward-sampling, exactly as for bvarm(sv = TRUE) (vignette("bayesian-var"), section 8). Wi∣h∼IG(1+T/2,kW2+12∑t(hit−hi,t−1)2)W_i\mid h\sim IG\big(1+T/2,\ k_W^2+\tfrac12\sum_t(h_{it}-h_{i,t-1})^2\big).
  4. Innovation covariances: Q∣βT∼IW(Q‾+∑t≥2ΔβtΔβt′,νQ+T−1)Q\mid\beta^T\sim IW\big(\bar Q+\sum_{t\ge2}\Delta\beta_t\Delta\beta_t',\ \nu_Q+T-1\big) and Si∣αT∼IW(S‾i+∑t≥2Δαi,tΔαi,t′,1+dim⁡Si+T−1)S_i\mid\alpha^T\sim IW\big(\bar S_i+\sum_{t\ge2}\Delta\alpha_{i,t}\Delta\alpha_{i,t}',\ 1+\dim S_i+T-1\big), with Q‾=kQ2νQV(B̂)\bar Q=k_Q^2\nu_QV(\hat B) the IW scale above. (With q_diag = TRUE, independent inverse-gamma priors on the diagonal of QQ replace the inverse-Wishart.)

The sweep touches the data TT times for each of K+K(K−1)/2+KK+K(K-1)/2+K state blocks, so it is linear in TT, and, because of step 1, roughly quadratic in mKmK. When a component is switched off (tv_beta = FALSE, tv_A = FALSE, sv = FALSE) the corresponding block is replaced by the conjugate Gaussian (or inverse-gamma, prior IG(3,2σ̂i2)IG(3,2\hat\sigma_i^2)) draw of a constant. The code is entirely in C++ and uses R’s random number generator, so set.seed() reproduces results.

What is stored. All draws of Q,S,WQ,S,W innovation standard deviations ($q_sd, $s_sd, $w_sd) and the posterior means of the paths ($beta_mean, $alpha_mean, $h_mean) use every retained draw; the full state paths of nsave_paths evenly spaced draws are kept ($beta: coefficients ×\times equations ×\times dates ×\times stored draws; $alpha, $h), and all impulse responses, volatilities and forecasts are computed from them. Memory is nsave_paths ×T×K(Kp+1)\times T\times K(Kp+1) doubles. (The number actually stored, glance(fit)$npaths, can be slightly below nsave_paths, because draws are spaced ceiling(ndraw / nsave_paths) apart.)

4. Outputs: coefficients, volatility, impulse responses, FEVD, forecasts

  • coef(fit, date = ): posterior mean (or median) of BtB_t at a date.
  • autoplot(fit, "coef", equation = ) / tidy(fit, "coef"): coefficient paths of one equation with credible bands (tibble columns date, response, term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high).
  • autoplot(fit, "vol") / tidy(fit, "vol") (= tvp_volatility(fit, "reduced")): the reduced-form residual standard deviation Σt,ii\sqrt{\Sigma_{t,ii}}, what a forecaster faces; "shock_vol" / "structural" (tidy(fit, "shock_vol")) gives ehit/2e^{h_{it}/2}, the sd of the orthogonalised shocks. The difference between the two is the contribution of the impact matrix AtA_t.
  • irf(fit, date = , horizon = ): impulse responses at a date with frozen parameters: Θh(t)=Φh(Bt)At−1Λt1/2,Φh=∑l=1min⁡(h,p)Al(t)Φh−l,Φ0=I, \Theta_h(t)=\Phi_h(B_t)\,A_t^{-1}\Lambda_t^{1/2},\qquad \Phi_h=\sum_{l=1}^{\min(h,p)}A_l(t)\Phi_{h-l},\ \Phi_0=I, the response of yt+hy_{t+h} to a one-standard-deviation recursive shock if the economy stayed at the date-tt parameters. This ignores the possibility that parameters change between tt and t+ht+h (generalised IRFs, which let them drift, would be different and wider) and mixes changes in propagation (Φh\Phi_h, AtA_t) with changes in the shock size (Λt\Lambda_t); normalise = list(shock = , variable = , size = ) fixes the impact response (for example 1 percentage point on the policy rate) and so isolates propagation. date is matched to the nearest element of fit$dates (calendar time if Y is a ts, else the row index); a date outside the estimation sample gives a warning and uses the nearest date. IRFs are recursive (Cholesky) only, and passing id = is an error (section 6.4).
  • irf_path(fit, shock, response, horizon, normalise_to): the response of one variable to one shock at a fixed horizon, as a function of the date; the usual “time-varying IRF” plot. Variables are tidyselect expressions (shock = rate); the result is a tibble (date, estimate, conf.low, conf.high), and autoplot(fit, "irf", shock = rate, response = inflation, horizon = c(0, 4, 8)) plots several horizons at once.
  • fevd(fit, date = ): the variance decomposition computed from the same frozen-parameter responses.
  • forecast(fit, h = , drift = TRUE): for every stored draw, the parameters are simulated forward as random walks with that draw’s Q,S,WQ,S,W and the path of yy follows; drift = FALSE freezes them at their last values.

5. Worked example: the Great Moderation and changing policy transmission

Quarterly US inflation, unemployment and a short-term interest rate, 1953-2006 (yraw). Variables are ordered as in the recursive identification of vignette("identification"): inflation, unemployment, rate (the interest rate shock is the last one, with a contemporaneous response of inflation and unemployment restricted to zero). We keep p=2p=2 and the default prior, and then vary kQ in section 6.

kqs <- c(0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1)
t_fit <- system.time(
  fits <- lapply(kqs, function(kq) tvpvar(yt, p = 2, ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500, nsave_paths = 200, prior = tvp_prior(kQ = kq))))
names(fits) <- kqs
fit <- fits[["0.01"]]                    # default prior
fit
#> <tvpvar> TVP-VAR(2), K = 3, estimation sample T = 173 (1963.5 - 2006.5), training tau = 40
#>   coefficients: time-varying; A_t: time-varying; volatility: stochastic
#>   1000 retained draws, 200 stored paths
round(unname(t_fit["elapsed"]) / 4, 1)   # seconds per fit
#> [1] 2.8
summary(fit)
#> <tvpvar> TVP-VAR(2), K = 3, estimation sample T = 173 (1963.5 - 2006.5), training tau = 40
#>   coefficients: time-varying; A_t: time-varying; volatility: stochastic
#>   1000 retained draws, 200 stored paths
#> Posterior mean innovation s.d. of the log-volatilities:
#>    inflation unemployment         rate 
#>       0.1778       0.2453       0.3108 
#> Median (over coefficients) posterior-mean s.d. of the coefficient drift sqrt(Q_jj): 0.00285
#> Range over time of the median reduced-form residual s.d.:
#>                min   max
#> inflation    0.140 0.572
#> unemployment 0.140 0.499
#> rate         0.268 2.044

The summary reports the posterior mean innovation standard deviation of the log-variance (about 0.20.2-0.30.3 per quarter: noticeable volatility drift), the median posterior standard deviation of the coefficient drift Qjj\sqrt{Q_{jj}} and the range over time of the median reduced-form residual standard deviation.

Volatility: the Great Moderation 

autoplot(fit, "vol")

vv <- tidy(fit, "vol")
vv$period <- ifelse(vv$date < 1984, "pre-1984", "post-1984")
round(tapply(vv$estimate, list(vv$variable, vv$period), mean)[c("inflation", "unemployment", "rate"), c("pre-1984", "post-1984")], 3)
#>              pre-1984 post-1984
#> inflation       0.387     0.211
#> unemployment    0.302     0.196
#> rate            0.844     0.432

The reduced-form volatility of all three series falls after the early 1980s (and that of the interest rate collapses from the Volcker disinflation of 1979-82), which is what the stochastic-volatility BVAR of vignette("bayesian-var") also finds. Whether the transmission changed is a different question, which requires βt\beta_t.

autoplot(fit, "shock_vol")

autoplot() returns an ordinary ggplot, and tidy() gives the same paths as a tibble, so custom versions are a few lines. For instance, the reduced-form volatility with its 90% band, on a common scale and with the Volcker disinflation marked:

tidy(fit, "vol", level = 0.90) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, estimate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1979.75, linetype = 3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = varm_palette(1), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  facet_wrap(~variable) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual standard deviation") +
  theme_varm()

Coefficients 

autoplot(fit, "coef", equation = rate)

The posterior median paths of the interest-rate equation vary little under the default prior. The summary above reports a median posterior sd of the drift of ≈0.003\approx 0.003 per quarter. That is equal to the prior, which should be read as a warning (section 6.1).

Impulse responses at two dates

Policy shock: a 1 percentage point increase in the interest rate (normalised impact), in 1975 (high and volatile inflation) and 2000 (the Great Moderation).

nr <- list(shock = "rate", variable = "rate", size = 1)
ir <- irf(fit, date = c(1975, 2000), horizon = 16, normalise = nr)
ir
#> <tvpvar_irf> responses at 2 dates: 1975, 2000
autoplot(ir[["1975"]], shocks = rate, responses = c(inflation, unemployment)) +
  labs(title = "1975")

autoplot(ir[["2000"]], shocks = rate, responses = c(inflation, unemployment)) +
  labs(title = "2000")

To overlay the two dates in one panel, bind the tidy() output of both (nested 68/90% bands, posterior medians as lines):

ov <- rbind(cbind(date = "1975", tidy(ir[["1975"]])), cbind(date = "2000", tidy(ir[["2000"]])))
ov <- subset(ov, shock == "rate" & response != "rate")
ggplot(ov, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = date, fill = date)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, group = interaction(date, level)), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(data = \(d) d[!duplicated(d[c("date", "response", "horizon")]), ], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~response, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) + scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (quarters)", y = "Response to a 1 pp rate shock", colour = "Date", fill = "Date") +
  theme_varm()

The responses of inflation and unemployment at a few horizons:

tab <- t(sapply(ir, function(z) c(infl_h4 = z$estimate["inflation", "rate", 5], infl_h8 = z$estimate["inflation", "rate", 9],
                                  unemp_h4 = z$estimate["unemployment", "rate", 5], unemp_h8 = z$estimate["unemployment", "rate", 9])))
round(tab, 3)
#>      infl_h4 infl_h8 unemp_h4 unemp_h8
#> 1975   -0.07  -0.132    0.023    0.075
#> 2000   -0.08  -0.175    0.019    0.086

Without normalisation, the responses also embed the size of the shock at each date (the standard deviation of the recursive interest-rate shock, eh3t/2e^{h_{3t}/2}, in the diagonal of the impact matrix):

ir_raw <- irf(fit, date = c(1975, 2000), horizon = 16)
round(sapply(ir_raw, function(z) z$estimate[, "rate", 1]), 3)     # impact responses to a one-sd rate shock
#>               1975  2000
#> inflation    0.000 0.000
#> unemployment 0.000 0.000
#> rate         0.684 0.369

The one-sd interest-rate shock in 1975 is about twice the size of the one in 2000. Comparing unnormalised responses across dates would then attribute a pure volatility change to a change in transmission.

Time-varying responses along the sample 

ip <- irf_path(fit, shock = "rate", response = "inflation", horizon = 8, normalise_to = "rate", size = 1, level = 0.68)
ip3 <- irf_path(fits[["0.03"]], shock = "rate", response = "inflation", horizon = 8, normalise_to = "rate", size = 1, level = 0.68)
rbind(cbind(kQ = "kQ = 0.01", ip), cbind(kQ = "kQ = 0.03", ip3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = varm_palette(1), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~kQ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Inflation response at h = 8 (rate shock, 1 pp)") +
  theme_varm()

irf_path() returns a tibble (class tvpvar_path; autoplot() of it gives a ggplot), so it is easy to customise. The comparison of the two panels is already the message of the next section: the shape of the time-varying response is driven by kQ at least as much as by the data.

Variance decomposition 

fe <- fevd(fit, date = c(1975, 2000), horizon = 12)
round(sapply(fe, function(z) z$estimate[, "rate", 13]), 3)   # share of the forecast-error variance (h = 12) due to the rate shock
#>               1975  2000
#> inflation    0.011 0.038
#> unemployment 0.011 0.018
#> rate         0.341 0.446

Rows are the variables, columns the dates: the fraction of the 12-quarter forecast-error variance of each variable explained by the recursive interest-rate shock.

Forecasting 

fc_d <- forecast(fit, h = 8, drift = TRUE)
fc_f <- forecast(fit, h = 8, drift = FALSE)
w <- function(fc, v) fc$bands[, v, "0.95"] - fc$bands[, v, "0.05"]
round(rbind(`drift = TRUE`  = w(fc_d, "rate")[c(1, 4, 8)], `drift = FALSE` = w(fc_f, "rate")[c(1, 4, 8)]), 2)  # 90% interval width, rate
#>               [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> drift = TRUE  0.88 2.48 3.96
#> drift = FALSE 0.94 2.49 3.79

With the default prior the two are practically the same (the differences are within Monte Carlo noise): over eight quarters the simulated drift of the coefficients is negligible next to shock uncertainty. drift = TRUE matters when kQ is large or volatility is changing fast. Because the end-of-sample volatility is low, both are narrower than a constant-volatility VAR would give (see vignette("bayesian-var"), section 8).

6. Pitfalls, and what the simulations say

6.1 The prior tightness drives the amount of time variation

The posterior of QQ is inverse-Wishart with scale Q‾+∑tΔβtΔβt′\bar Q+\sum_t\Delta\beta_t\Delta\beta_t' and νQ+T−1\nu_Q+T-1 degrees of freedom, so the data speak about QQ only through the quarter-to-quarter changes of the smoothed state paths. Those changes are small relative to the sampling noise of each coefficient, and the paths are themselves drawn under the current QQ: a small QQ gives smooth paths, hence a small sum of squared changes, hence a small QQ. The prior counts for νQ=40\nu_Q=40 observations against T−1=172T-1=172 of data, and in practice the posterior of QQ stays close to the prior. Check it: if the data were informative, the posterior sd of the drift would not move one-for-one with kQ.

nb <- fit$m * fit$K
dead <- function(f) { # share of stored draws with a root on or outside the unit circle at some date
  p <- f$p; K <- f$K; N <- dim(f$beta)[4]
  mean(sapply(seq_len(N), function(n) any(sapply(seq_len(f$T), function(t) {
    B <- f$beta[1:(K * p), , t, n]
    max(Mod(eigen(rbind(t(B), cbind(diag(K * (p - 1)), matrix(0, K * (p - 1), K))), only.values = TRUE)$values)) >= 1 }))))
}
kq_tab <- t(sapply(fits, function(f) {
  pq <- sqrt(diag(f$prior_values$Qbar) / (f$prior_values$nuQ - nb - 1))
  ir2 <- irf(f, date = c(1975, 2000), horizon = 12, normalise = nr)
  c(`prior sd of drift` = median(pq), `posterior sd of drift` = median(sqrt(colMeans(f$q_sd^2))),
    `max range of mean path` = max(apply(f$beta_mean, 1:2, function(v) diff(range(v)))),
    `infl. resp. h=8, 1975` = ir2[[1]]$estimate["inflation", "rate", 9], `infl. resp. h=8, 2000` = ir2[[2]]$estimate["inflation", "rate", 9],
    `share explosive` = dead(f))
}))
rownames(kq_tab) <- paste0("kQ = ", kqs)
round(kq_tab, 4)
#>            prior sd of drift posterior sd of drift max range of mean path
#> kQ = 0.003            0.0007                0.0007                 0.0052
#> kQ = 0.01             0.0025                0.0025                 0.0532
#> kQ = 0.03             0.0074                0.0075                 0.1586
#> kQ = 0.1              0.0247                0.0234                 0.4507
#>            infl. resp. h=8, 1975 infl. resp. h=8, 2000 share explosive
#> kQ = 0.003               -0.1413               -0.1469           0.070
#> kQ = 0.01                -0.1323               -0.1755           0.115
#> kQ = 0.03                -0.0006               -0.1884           0.450
#> kQ = 0.1                  0.2607               -0.1556           0.985

Read across the rows. The posterior standard deviation of the drift is 0.99 times the prior standard deviation in every row (median ratio): the data barely update QQ, so Q̂\hat Q is whatever kQ says. As a result everything downstream moves with it: the coefficient paths range over 0.005 (kQ = 0.003), 0.053 (default), 0.159 and 0.451 (kQ = 0.1) (maximum over coefficients of the range of the posterior mean path), and the 8-quarter response of inflation to a 1 pp rate shock in 1975 is -0.14, -0.13, 0 and 0.26 (compare 2000: -0.15, -0.18, -0.19, -0.16). With the default prior there is essentially no change in transmission between 1975 and 2000; at kQ=0.03k_Q=0.03 the 1975 response is about zero and the 2000 response is negative; at kQ=0.1k_Q=0.1 the 1975 response is a “price puzzle” (inflation rises after a tightening), which is the kind of finding that appears in the literature. A sample cannot tell these apart, and the last column shows the cost of looser priors: a growing share of the posterior draws with an explosive root at some date.

The package’s own validation says the same. validation/tvp.R simulates TVP-VAR-SV data with known paths and measures the coverage of the 90% credible bands of the coefficient paths under the data-driven training-sample prior: with the default prior (kQ = 0.01) and with kQ = 0.05 the coverage is 0.56-0.79 (8 replications of T=250T=250, K=3K=3), well below 0.90, because the prior is too tight for the DGP, whereas when the data are simulated from the prior the sampler itself is calibrated (coverage about 0.90). The sampler is correct; the prior is informative. A small version of that experiment (the DGP of the validation script; three replications, so noisy):

sim_tvp <- function(T = 200, K = 3, qb = 0.012, qa = 0.03, qh = 0.08) {   # p = 1 TVP-VAR-SV with known paths
  m <- K + 1; nb <- m * K; beta <- matrix(0, nb, T)
  b <- as.numeric(rbind(diag(0.6, K), c(0.2, 0.1, 0.1))); a <- c(0.3, -0.2, 0.2); hh <- log(c(0.3, 0.2, 0.25)^2)
  Y <- matrix(0, T, K); y <- rep(0, K)
  for (t in 1:T) {
    b <- b + qb * rnorm(nb); a <- a + qa * rnorm(3); hh <- hh + qh * rnorm(K)
    A <- diag(K); A[2, 1] <- a[1]; A[3, 1] <- a[2]; A[3, 2] <- a[3]
    y <- as.numeric(c(y, 1) %*% matrix(b, m, K) + solve(A, exp(hh / 2) * rnorm(K))); Y[t, ] <- y; beta[, t] <- b
  }
  colnames(Y) <- c("a", "b", "c"); list(Y = Y, beta = beta)
}
cover <- function(kq, nrep = 3) {
  cv <- numeric(0)
  for (r in seq_len(nrep)) {
    d <- sim_tvp(); if (max(abs(d$Y)) > 50) next
    f <- tvpvar(d$Y, p = 1, ndraw = 600, nburn = 400, nsave_paths = 200, prior = tvp_prior(tau = 40, kQ = kq))
    tb <- array(d$beta[, 42:200], dim(f$beta)[1:3]); bq <- apply(f$beta, 1:3, quantile, probs = c(0.05, 0.95))
    cv <- c(cv, mean(tb >= bq[1, , , ] & tb <= bq[2, , , ]))
  }
  mean(cv)
}
set.seed(5)
round(c(`kQ = 0.01 (default)` = cover(0.01), `kQ = 0.05` = cover(0.05)), 2)   # nominal 0.90
#> kQ = 0.01 (default)           kQ = 0.05 
#>                0.55                0.76

What to do about it: (i) report results for several kQ (as in the table above) and show that the conclusion you draw is robust; (ii) compare with the constant-coefficient benchmark (tv_beta = FALSE; below); (iii) use out-of-sample density forecasts or the marginal likelihood of the competing models (not provided by tvpvar(); this is a limitation) rather than the plausibility of the paths; (iv) if the economics gives you a prior on how fast coefficients move, put it into kQ, but state it.

6.2 The constant-parameter limit

As kQ,kS,kW→0k_Q,k_S,k_W\to0 the model collapses to a constant-parameter VAR. This is a sanity check of the sampler (and a useful property): with essentially degenerate state innovations, diffuse initial states (vscale large) and constant variance, the posterior mean of the coefficients at every date converges to OLS on the estimation sample, and the paths are flat. The comparison below uses the real data:

p <- 2; tau <- 40
ols <- varm(as.matrix(yraw)[(tau + 1):nrow(yraw), ], p = p)               # OLS on the estimation sample
pr0 <- tvp_prior(tau = tau, kQ = 1e-6, kS = 1e-6, kW = 1e-6, vscale = 1e4)
f_q0 <- tvpvar(yt, p, ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500, nsave_paths = 100, sv = FALSE, tv_A = FALSE, prior = pr0)
f_c  <- tvpvar(yt, p, ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500, nsave_paths = 100, sv = FALSE, tv_beta = FALSE, tv_A = FALSE, prior = pr0)
round(c(`max |mean - OLS|, kQ = 1e-6`        = max(abs(coef(f_q0, date = "last") - ols$B)),
        `max |mean - OLS|, tv_beta = FALSE`  = max(abs(coef(f_c,  date = "last") - ols$B)),
        `max time variation of mean path, kQ = 1e-6` = max(apply(f_q0$beta_mean, 1:2, function(v) diff(range(v))))), 4)
#>                max |mean - OLS|, kQ = 1e-6 
#>                                     0.0072 
#>          max |mean - OLS|, tv_beta = FALSE 
#>                                     0.0049 
#> max time variation of mean path, kQ = 1e-6 
#>                                     0.0000

(The first two are Monte Carlo error of a 1000-draw posterior mean; the last is zero to numerical precision.) The constant limit is also where the standard deviation of the OLS estimates comes from: the posterior sd at the last date of the kQ~0 model is the exact GLS sd (the package validation checks this to within Monte Carlo error).

6.3 Time variation found where there is none

The second experiment generates data with constant coefficients and fits the TVP-VAR with two values of kQ. Three DGPs, all with truth equal to a constant coefficient matrix: (a) homoskedastic Gaussian shocks; (b) volatility that drops by two thirds half-way through the sample (a Great-Moderation-like break; the model has SV, so it should absorb it); (c) the same as (a) with two shocks 6 times larger than usual, a stand-in for Gaussian misspecification (outliers, a crisis episode). In each case the only time variation in the truth is in the volatility (b). We report the largest, over the 21 coefficients, of the range over time of the posterior-mean path (the truth is 0):

sim_const <- function(T = 215, kind = c("gauss", "break", "outlier")) {
  kind <- match.arg(kind); K <- 3
  B1 <- matrix(c(.8, .1, 0, 0, .7, .1, .1, 0, .8), 3, byrow = TRUE); c0 <- c(.2, .1, .2)
  Ai <- solve(matrix(c(1, 0, 0, .3, 1, 0, -.2, .2, 1), 3, byrow = TRUE))
  sc <- rep(1, T + 50); if (kind == "break") sc[51:(50 + T %/% 2)] <- 3
  Y <- matrix(0, T + 50, K)
  for (t in 2:(T + 50)) {
    e <- Ai %*% (sc[t] * c(.5, .4, .6) * rnorm(3))
    if (kind == "outlier" && t %in% (50 + c(60, 130))) e <- e * 6
    Y[t, ] <- c0 + B1 %*% Y[t - 1, ] + e
  }
  ts(`colnames<-`(Y[-(1:50), ], c("a", "b", "c")), start = 1953, frequency = 4)
}
set.seed(10)
sp <- sapply(c("gauss", "break", "outlier"), function(kind) {
  Y <- sim_const(kind = kind)
  sapply(c(0.01, 0.05), function(kq) {
    f <- tvpvar(Y, p = 2, ndraw = 800, nburn = 400, nsave_paths = 100, prior = tvp_prior(kQ = kq))
    max(apply(f$beta_mean, 1:2, function(v) diff(range(v))))
  })
})
dimnames(sp) <- list(c("kQ = 0.01", "kQ = 0.05"), c("(a) Gaussian", "(b) variance break", "(c) outliers"))
round(sp, 3)
#>           (a) Gaussian (b) variance break (c) outliers
#> kQ = 0.01        0.023              0.042        0.020
#> kQ = 0.05        0.163              0.341        0.325

With the default prior the estimated paths are nearly flat in every DGP (the largest range is 0.04; for scale, the VAR coefficients are of order 0.1-0.8). With kQ = 0.05 the model reports substantial movement of the coefficients, 0.16 even for well-behaved Gaussian data, and 0.34 and 0.32 with a variance break and with two outliers, although nothing changed in the coefficients. Two points. (i) Stochastic volatility does not make the problem go away: in (b) the model has SV and still attributes part of the change in the size of the shocks to coefficient drift, because the break is large and kQ is loose. (ii) Outliers have the same effect, since a constant coefficient cannot explain a 6-sigma shock but a drifting one can. Hence the advice in section 6.1, plus: check residuals for outliers before reading anything into coefficient paths, and compare to tv_beta = FALSE, asking whether the normalised IRFs differ across dates by more than their bands.

# benchmark: constant coefficients, stochastic volatility (a BVAR with SV); normalised IRFs at the two dates
f_b <- tvpvar(yt, p = 2, ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500, nsave_paths = 200, tv_beta = FALSE)
ib <- irf(f_b, date = c(1975, 2000), horizon = 12, normalise = nr)
round(rbind(`constant B, 1975` = ib[[1]]$estimate["inflation", "rate", c(5, 9)], `constant B, 2000` = ib[[2]]$estimate["inflation", "rate", c(5, 9)],
            `TVP (default), 1975` = ir[[1]]$estimate["inflation", "rate", c(5, 9)], `TVP (default), 2000` = ir[[2]]$estimate["inflation", "rate", c(5, 9)]), 3)
#>                          4      8
#> constant B, 1975    -0.074 -0.152
#> constant B, 2000    -0.074 -0.152
#> TVP (default), 1975 -0.070 -0.132
#> TVP (default), 2000 -0.080 -0.175

With constant BB the normalised responses at the two dates coincide to the displayed precision: they could differ only through AtA_t, which barely moves. The TVP rows differ from them and from each other, but by an amount that is small relative to the posterior bands of the previous section (compare the first plot there). Under the default prior, then, the data support “no big change in transmission”, and more time variation only appears when the prior is loosened (section 6.1).

6.4 Recursive identification only

irf() and fevd() for a tvpvar always use the recursive (Cholesky) scheme in the order of the columns of Y, because the model is parametrised through a triangular AtA_t and a diagonal Λt\Lambda_t. There is no id = argument: passing one is an error (irf(fit, id = id_chol()) aborts, even for the Cholesky scheme). Sign restrictions, proxies and long-run restrictions with time-varying parameters need a different rotation of each draw’s Σt\Sigma_t and are not implemented. Also, in the TVP-VAR-SV the ordering matters for the model, not only for the interpretation (the random-walk dynamics are specified on the Cholesky factors), which is the same issue as the ordering caveat in vignette("bayesian-var"), section 6. Re-estimate with another ordering and compare.

6.5 reject_explosive: what it does and what it does not do

Random-walk coefficient paths are not constrained to the stationary region, so some draws have a companion matrix with a root on or outside the unit circle at some dates. In the default fit above 12% of the stored draws have such a date, at kQ=0.03k_Q=0.03 45% and at kQ=0.1k_Q=0.1 98%. (Explosive roots over a few quarters are not implausible for inflation and interest rates in the 1970s, which is why this is not an error.) The frozen-parameter IRFs at such a date diverge. reject_explosive = TRUE imposes the Cogley and Sargent (2005) stability truncation as follows: each time the coefficient path is drawn (step 1), the whole path is redrawn, up to max_tries times, until all dates have a stable companion matrix; if no stable path is found in max_tries draws, the previous path is kept. Consequences:

  • it is slow: the effective cost per sweep is up to max_tries path draws; at kQ=0.05k_Q=0.05 the runtime of a fit with T=173T=173 rose from about 4 s to about 13 s (3 times) in our test;
  • it is only an approximation to the truncated posterior when the retry cap binds, and when most draws are explosive (large kQ) the chain can stay on one path for several sweeps, which inflates autocorrelation (check mcmc_diagnostics() on $q_sd);
  • it truncates the prior on βT\beta^T as well as the posterior, so it is a modelling assumption (stationarity of every date) and not a convergence device; it changes what you learn about persistence in the data (the 1970s inflation process may not be stationary), and it is no substitute for choosing kQ sensibly;
  • only βt\beta_t is truncated: the initial state is not checked.
f_rej <- tvpvar(yt, p = 2, ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500, prior = tvp_prior(kQ = 0.03), reject_explosive = TRUE, max_tries = 10)

6.6 Convergence and computation

The state paths themselves move a lot between sweeps, but the innovation scales WiW_i of the log-volatilities, and with them the smoothness of the volatility paths, mix slowly, as does the amount of drift. Use mcmc_diagnostics() on the stored innovation standard deviations ($w_sd, $q_sd):

dg <- mcmc_diagnostics(cbind(w_inflation = fit$w_sd[, 1], w_unemployment = fit$w_sd[, 2], w_rate = fit$w_sd[, 3],
                             q_drift_median = apply(fit$q_sd, 1, median)))
dg
#>            term estimate std.error  ess rhat geweke_z
#>     w_inflation  0.17781  0.045102 21.2 1.02   0.5183
#>  w_unemployment  0.24528  0.126077 13.9 1.00   0.2852
#>          w_rate  0.31082  0.076785 26.0 1.06  -3.5351
#>  q_drift_median  0.00243  0.000227 81.2 1.00  -0.0347

With the ndraw = 1000 of this vignette the effective sample sizes of the log-volatility innovation scales are only about 14-26: the posterior means of the volatility paths are fine (they average over many dates), but credible intervals for WiW_i need 10000 or more draws, and you should run two chains with different seeds and compare R̂\hat R.

Typical cost: a sweep with all of SV, time-varying AtA_t and a full QQ at K=3K=3, p=2p=2 (estimation sample T=173T=173) takes well under a millisecond to a few milliseconds depending on the machine. Timing a longer run of 10000 retained draws plus 2000 burn-in on the machine that built this vignette:

t_long <- system.time(tvpvar(yt, p = 2, ndraw = 10000, nburn = 2000))[["elapsed"]]
c(seconds = t_long, ms_per_sweep = 1000 * t_long / 12000)
#>      seconds ms_per_sweep 
#>    21.956000     1.829667

The cost is linear in TT and increases quickly with the state dimension K(Kp+1)K(Kp+1): with p=4p=4 ($n_eta=39$) it is several times larger. Keep pp small (2 for quarterly data is standard in this literature) and the number of variables at 3-4; larger TVP-VARs need dimension reduction or shrinkage that this implementation does not offer. For the number of paths stored see nsave_paths.

7. Summary of practical advice

  1. Fit the default prior and several values of kQ (0.003-0.1), the constant-coefficient SV benchmark (tv_beta = FALSE) and compare the normalised impulse responses at the dates of interest.
  2. Check whether the posterior of the drift scale (Qjj\sqrt{Q_{jj}}, $q_sd) differs from the prior (kQ×k_Q\times OLS s.e.); if not, the amount of time variation is an assumption.
  3. Always allow stochastic volatility; omitted heteroskedasticity is absorbed by coefficient drift. Inspect residuals for outliers.
  4. Use normalise = to compare propagation across dates and irf_path() to see the whole history; remember the frozen-parameter definition.
  5. Keep pp and KK small, and remember that the first tau observations are used up by the prior.
